title: A library of sutras
hookLine: the Mahayana sutras are many; we read a handful, paraphrased

lines: ONE BOOK ON A LONG SHELF.
cards: "Thus have I heard." That's how the discourses open in the old English of Rhys Davids, before anyone is named, before a place or a crowd. For weeks this path has stayed inside one book, the Lotus.

Today i'm stepping out of it with you to look at the shelf it sits on. It's a long shelf. The Mahayana sutras are many, kept in Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan, and loved in different places for different reasons.
Over the coming weeks i'll open a handful.

teach.h: A SUTRA IS A DISCOURSE IN A SCENE.
teach.b: Start with the word. A sutra is a discourse: a teaching set in a scene, with a place, a crowd, and someone asking a question.

teach.h: THUS HAVE I HEARD: ANANDA'S WORDS.
teach.b: Tradition says that after the Buddha died, his attendant Ananda recited what he had heard, which is why the discourses open with those words.
The Mahayana sutras open the same way, and then the scenes grow huge: assemblies of bodhisattvas, light pouring from the Buddha's brow, worlds beyond counting.

teach.h: WHO HOLDS THESE BOOKS, AND HOW.
teach.b: Different Buddhists hold these books differently, so here, plainly, is who holds what. Mahayana traditions in China, Tibet, Korea, Japan and Vietnam receive these sutras as the Buddha's word.

The Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia keeps its own canon in Pali, and these Mahayana sutras aren't part of it. Historians tell their own story about when and where the texts were written.
This path tells each text as it tells itself, and names the differences without ranking anyone.
Now the shelf ahead. A sick layman in the city of Vaishali who out-talks the Buddha's great disciples, and a goddess who scatters flowers in his room.
A sutra that pictures the universe as a net of jewels, and a young pilgrim who visits teacher after teacher. A finger pointing at the moon.
A Buddha of medicine, a bodhisattva who vows to empty the hells, and a queen named Srimala who teaches.
One honest note: i'll mostly retell these in my own words, because the English translations i'd want to quote aren't ones i can share freely. When i paraphrase, i'll say so.

how: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia, Tibet and Vietnam chant, study and copy sutras such as the Lotus, the Heart Sutra and the Vimalakirti, and each school tends to center a few of them; the Theravada tradition keeps the Pali canon instead.

games.q: you're Ananda, asked to pass on what the Buddha taught. how do you begin?
o: with your own summary of the main points.
with the words: thus have I heard.
with a list of rules for monks.
games.why: tradition sets those words in Ananda's mouth: not a claim to be clever, just a witness passing on what reached him.

practice: Say those four words silently once: thus have I heard. Notice that they don't claim to be clever; they say, I was there, and I'm passing on what reached me.
Then sit the way you'd sit at the start of a story, listening, and let the sounds in the room be the opening scene.

wordCard.voice: A library of sutras. Many discourses, each opening with thus have I heard, held differently by different Buddhists. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: thus by me it was heard. the opening line of a sutra.

carryVoice: Your line: a library. Every book on it begins by saying where it came from. Eleven hundred eighty-five days, and counting.
